distractorExplanations.a: Swaps Improve/Control for Design/Verify; that is DMADV (Design for Six Sigma) for new processes, not DMAIC.
distractorExplanations.b: Starts with Design; DMAIC opens by defining the problem, scope and CTQs before any solution is designed.
distractorExplanations.c: Assess, Implement and Confirm are invented phase names; the real DMAIC phases are Analyze, Improve and Control.

options.a: Baseline data, gage R&R, process capability

distractorExplanations.a: Baseline data, gage R&R and capability are Measure-phase deliverables, done after Define has set scope.
distractorExplanations.c: Verifying root causes with hypothesis tests is the Analyze phase, two phases after Define.
distractorExplanations.d: Piloting, control plans and handover belong to Improve and Control, the last two DMAIC phases.

options.a: Rank failure modes by severity, occurrence, detection
options.b: Detail every process step with decision diamonds
options.c: Sort defect categories from most to least frequent
options.d: Map suppliers, inputs, process, outputs, customers

distractorExplanations.a: Ranking failure modes by S/O/D describes an FMEA, not a SIPOC high-level process map.
distractorExplanations.b: A SIPOC is a high-level 4-7 step view; step-by-step decision diamonds are a detailed flowchart.
distractorExplanations.c: Sorting defect categories by frequency is a Pareto chart, not a SIPOC scoping map.

distractorExplanations.a: Generating and testing root-cause hypotheses is the Analyze phase, which follows Measure.
distractorExplanations.b: Piloting solutions and weighing cost-benefit happens in Improve, after the baseline is set.
distractorExplanations.c: Response plans and process audits sustain gains in the Control phase, not in Measure.

options.b: Baseline sigma level of the process

distractorExplanations.b: Establishing the baseline sigma level is a Measure-phase output that Analyze builds on.
distractorExplanations.c: Sponsor sign-off on scope is a Define-phase charter task, not the purpose of Analyze.
distractorExplanations.d: Controls to sustain gains are the Control phase; Analyze finds and verifies root causes.

distractorExplanations.b: Baseline capability indices are calculated in Measure, before any countermeasure exists.
distractorExplanations.c: Gage repeatability studies (MSA) validate the measurement system in the Measure phase.
distractorExplanations.d: Root-cause hypotheses are tested in Analyze; Improve tests solutions that address them.

options.a: Gains via standards, monitoring, response plans
options.b: Gains via one-time final inspection of output
options.c: Gains via the project team running the process
options.d: Gains via retraining only when customers complain

distractorExplanations.b: One-time final inspection detects defects but does not hold the process; Control uses ongoing monitoring.
distractorExplanations.c: Control hands the process to the process owner; the project team does not keep running it.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting for customer complaints is reactive; a control plan triggers action on process signals.

options.a: Detailed root-cause analysis and verified Xs
options.b: Business case, scope, goals, timeline, team
options.c: Final control plan and response procedures
options.d: Chosen solution and full implementation plan

distractorExplanations.a: Verified root causes (Xs) come out of Analyze; the charter is written before analysis starts.
distractorExplanations.c: The control plan and response procedures are Control-phase deliverables, not charter content.
distractorExplanations.d: A charter should not presuppose a solution; solutions are selected in the Improve phase.

options.a: Cost to Quality internal spending targets
options.d: Critical to Quantity production volume goals

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses CTQ with Cost of Quality (COQ), which tracks prevention, appraisal and failure costs.
distractorExplanations.b: Process control limits come from control charts; CTQ is a customer requirement, not a limit.
distractorExplanations.d: CTQ stands for Critical to Quality, a measurable customer need, not a production volume goal.

distractorExplanations.a: Ease of measurement does not make a metric primary; the primary metric must be the project Y.
distractorExplanations.b: Inputs (Xs) are potential causes; the primary metric measures the output Y the project improves.
distractorExplanations.d: Consequential (secondary) metrics guard against side effects; they are not the primary metric.

options.b: Set control limits for the Y

distractorExplanations.a: Ranking root causes by impact is Pareto/Analyze work; stakeholder analysis maps people and influence.
distractorExplanations.b: Control limits are calculated from process data on a control chart, not from stakeholder analysis.
distractorExplanations.d: Financial benefits are estimated by finance/benefit tracking; stakeholder analysis targets buy-in.

distractorExplanations.b: Control limits are computed on control charts; a tollgate reviews whether a phase is complete.
distractorExplanations.c: Gage accuracy is checked in an MSA during Measure; the tollgate reviews phase deliverables overall.
distractorExplanations.d: Defect counts are data collected in Measure; a tollgate is a go/no-go review of phase readiness.

options.a: Lead projects part-time with Black Belt support
options.b: Lead projects full-time and coach Black Belts
options.c: Set strategy and select the project portfolio
options.d: Mentor Black Belts on advanced statistics

distractorExplanations.b: Full-time project leadership describes a Black Belt; coaching Black Belts is the Master Black Belt role.
distractorExplanations.c: Setting strategy and choosing the portfolio is the Champion/executive role, not a Green Belt duty.
distractorExplanations.d: Mentoring Black Belts on advanced statistics is a Master Black Belt responsibility.

options.a: A unit with one or more errors
options.d: A chance for an error to occur

distractorExplanations.a: A unit with one or more errors is a defective; a defect is each individual failure to meet a requirement.
distractorExplanations.c: Variation within specification is not a defect; only failing a requirement counts as a defect.
distractorExplanations.d: A chance for an error to occur is an opportunity, the denominator in DPO/DPMO, not a defect.

distractorExplanations.a: Defectives per million units is PPM; DPMO counts defects against opportunities, not units.
distractorExplanations.c: Dividing by units gives DPU x 1,000,000; DPMO divides by units times opportunities per unit.
distractorExplanations.d: DPMO is a rate per million opportunities, not a time-based count per month of operation.

options.a: Skewed right; used to model counts of rare events
options.b: Bell-shaped; many tools assume approximate normality
options.c: Flat; every value in the range equally likely
options.d: Bimodal; it signals two mixed process streams

distractorExplanations.a: Right-skewed counts of rare events describe the Poisson distribution, not the symmetric normal curve.
distractorExplanations.c: Equal likelihood across a range is the uniform distribution; the normal is peaked at the mean.
distractorExplanations.d: A bimodal shape signals mixed streams and is non-normal; the normal distribution has one peak.

options.a: Distinguish unusual signals from routine variation
options.b: Distinguish operator errors from machine errors
options.c: Separate variation inside vs outside spec limits

distractorExplanations.b: Special vs common cause is about signal type, not whether a person or a machine produced it.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses specification limits with control limits; special causes are judged against control limits.
distractorExplanations.d: Short- vs long-term capability (Cp vs Pp) is a capability concept, not the special/common distinction.

options.b: Compare output to customer spec limits

distractorExplanations.b: Comparing output to spec limits is capability analysis; control charts use process-derived limits.
distractorExplanations.c: Ranking defect types by frequency is a Pareto chart, not a control chart.
distractorExplanations.d: Correlation between two variables is shown on a scatter plot, not a control chart.

options.a: The probability that the null hypothesis is true
options.b: Evidence against a null hypothesis in context
options.c: Size of the practical effect observed
options.d: Power to detect a true difference

distractorExplanations.a: Classic misreading: the p-value is the probability of data this extreme if H0 is true, not P(H0 true).
distractorExplanations.c: Effect size measures practical magnitude; a tiny p-value can accompany a trivial effect.
distractorExplanations.d: Power (1 - beta) is the chance of detecting a real difference; it is set by n, alpha and effect size.

distractorExplanations.a: A larger sample reduces random error, not bias; biased sampling stays biased at any sample size.
distractorExplanations.b: Normality and capability are data properties, not what you trade off when choosing sample size.
distractorExplanations.d: Alpha is chosen separately and process stability is checked on charts; neither is the n tradeoff.

options.b: Process capability Cp/Cpk against spec limits
options.c: Process stability via X-bar/R control charts
options.d: Sample size and power for hypothesis tests

distractorExplanations.b: Cp/Cpk measure the process against specs; MSA checks the gage first so capability data can be trusted.
distractorExplanations.c: X-bar/R charts monitor process stability; MSA evaluates the measurement system, not the process.
distractorExplanations.d: Sample size and power are planning steps for hypothesis tests, not measurement system checks.

options.b: Every population value to the target
options.c: Data to a claim about a population
options.d: Expert opinions to a stated benchmark

distractorExplanations.a: Comparing control limits to spec limits is a capability view, not a statistical hypothesis test.
distractorExplanations.b: Measuring every population value is a census; hypothesis tests infer from a sample to a population.
distractorExplanations.d: Hypothesis tests use sample data, not expert opinion, to judge a claim about a population.

options.a: Prove that X causes the Y

distractorExplanations.a: Regression shows association; causation needs a designed experiment or process knowledge.
distractorExplanations.b: Comparing two variances is an F-test (or Levene), not regression modeling of Y on X.
distractorExplanations.d: Ranking defects by count is a Pareto chart; regression fits an equation linking Y to Xs.

options.b: Customer data vs process data from gages
options.d: Sampled data vs data from a full census

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the definitions: attribute data are counts/categories and variable data are continuous.
distractorExplanations.b: Customer vs process data describes the source, not the attribute/variable data type.
distractorExplanations.d: Sample vs census describes how data were collected, not whether they are attribute or variable.

distractorExplanations.a: An operational definition aims at consistency between collectors, not speed of data collection.
distractorExplanations.c: Spec limits come from the customer; an operational definition only defines how to measure.
distractorExplanations.d: Significance comes from hypothesis tests; operational definitions make the measurements consistent.

distractorExplanations.b: Defect frequencies are displayed on a Pareto chart; a fishbone organizes potential causes by category.
distractorExplanations.c: Process steps in sequence are a flowchart or process map, not an Ishikawa diagram.
distractorExplanations.d: Failure mode scores (RPN) belong to FMEA; the fishbone groups causes under 6M-type headings.

distractorExplanations.a: 5 Whys drills down one causal chain; it does not list five parallel candidate causes.
distractorExplanations.c: 5 Whys targets process causes; stopping at a person to blame is the classic misuse of the tool.
distractorExplanations.d: Containment stops the bleeding quickly; 5 Whys digs past symptoms to the underlying root cause.

distractorExplanations.a: Trends over time are shown on a run or control chart; Pareto bars are sorted by size, not time.
distractorExplanations.b: Spread versus specification is a histogram/capability view, not a Pareto chart.
distractorExplanations.d: Correlation between X and Y is a scatter plot; a Pareto chart ranks categories by contribution.

options.b: Root causes by count, as on a Pareto chart

distractorExplanations.a: FMEA's RPN uses severity, occurrence and detection; cost and customer impact are not the three factors.
distractorExplanations.b: Ranking causes by count is Pareto analysis; FMEA scores potential failure modes before they occur.
distractorExplanations.d: Value-added vs non-value-added time is value stream analysis, not FMEA risk prioritization.

options.b: Supplier-to-customer scope at a high level
options.c: Detailed task steps for one operator

distractorExplanations.a: Reporting lines and responsibilities are an org chart or RACI, not a value stream map.
distractorExplanations.b: A high-level supplier-to-customer scope is a SIPOC; a VSM adds flow, wait times and waste.
distractorExplanations.c: Detailed task steps for one operator are standard work or a detailed flowchart, not a VSM.

distractorExplanations.a: Ranking causes by frequency is a Pareto chart, which may use check-sheet data but is a different tool.
distractorExplanations.b: Testing differences in means needs a t-test or ANOVA; a check sheet only records the data.
distractorExplanations.c: Mapping cause categories is a fishbone diagram; a check sheet tallies observations as they occur.

options.c: Proof that one variable causes another

distractorExplanations.a: The frequency distribution of a single variable is a histogram; a scatter plot needs paired data.
distractorExplanations.c: A scatter plot shows correlation only; correlation does not prove causation.
distractorExplanations.d: Ranking defect categories is a Pareto chart, not a scatter plot of two variables.

distractorExplanations.a: Final inspection detects defects after they occur; poka-yoke prevents the error from happening.
distractorExplanations.c: Retraining after errors relies on memory and vigilance; poka-yoke designs the error out.
distractorExplanations.d: Spec limits are customer requirements; tightening them prevents nothing at the process step.

distractorExplanations.b: Standard work captures today's best known method, not an idealized future state from a VSM.
distractorExplanations.c: Standard work replaces individual methods with one agreed best method so results are consistent.
distractorExplanations.d: Design specs define the product; standard work defines the sequence, timing and WIP of the task.

distractorExplanations.a: A kaizen event is a short (often 3-5 day) blitz, not a months-long DMAIC project.
distractorExplanations.b: A daily huddle is a communication routine; a kaizen event is a dedicated improvement workshop.
distractorExplanations.c: An annual strategic review sets direction; a kaizen event makes rapid changes at the gemba.

options.a: Vote on each idea as raised

distractorExplanations.a: Voting comes after idea generation (e.g., multivoting); judging each idea live stifles output.
distractorExplanations.b: Brainstorming seeks quantity, including untested ideas; proving causes comes later in Analyze.
distractorExplanations.c: Letting experts lead anchors the group; brainstorming gives every member equal voice.

distractorExplanations.a: Grouping defects by frequency is a Pareto chart; affinity diagrams cluster ideas by theme.
distractorExplanations.c: Swim lanes organize process steps by owner in a deployment flowchart, not an affinity diagram.
distractorExplanations.d: Ranking risks by RPN is FMEA; an affinity diagram sorts qualitative ideas into natural groups.

distractorExplanations.a: A pilot tests a solution; a control plan is still needed to sustain it after full rollout.
distractorExplanations.b: Root causes are verified in Analyze; the pilot tests whether the solution works at small scale.
distractorExplanations.d: The baseline is set in Measure before any solution; a pilot compares results against it.

options.a: Project scope, goals, team, and timeline
options.b: What/who/how often to monitor and react
options.c: Failure modes ranked by RPN for each step

distractorExplanations.a: Scope, goals, team and timeline are the project charter from Define, not the control plan.
distractorExplanations.c: RPN-ranked failure modes are an FMEA; the control plan may reference it but lists monitoring actions.
distractorExplanations.d: Verified root causes are Analyze outputs; the control plan says how controls are monitored and owned.

distractorExplanations.a: A response plan is triggered by out-of-control signals, not by customer specification changes.
distractorExplanations.b: Charter approval by the sponsor happens in Define; response plans live in the control plan.
distractorExplanations.c: Pilot rollout planning is Improve work; response plans tell owners how to react to signals.

distractorExplanations.a: Keeping original SOPs in use is the failure document control prevents; old revisions are withdrawn.
distractorExplanations.b: Document control governs versions and access, not reducing how many documents exist.
distractorExplanations.d: Approval speed is not the goal; document control ensures only the current approved version is used.

distractorExplanations.a: Training remains required after the pilot; untrained operators drift back to the old method.
distractorExplanations.b: Existing operators must also learn the new standard, not just new hires joining later.
distractorExplanations.c: An email notice is not training; people need demonstration and practice to adopt standard work.

distractorExplanations.a: Visual management shows real-time status at the workplace, not longer monthly reports.
distractorExplanations.c: Visual controls support the control plan; they do not replace its owners and reaction steps.
distractorExplanations.d: Visual management is about instant shared awareness, not simplifying statistical calculation.

distractorExplanations.b: Certification is a personal credential; handover transfers process ownership to the process owner.
distractorExplanations.c: Charter approval happens at the start in Define; handover is the close of Control.
distractorExplanations.d: A new baseline is set in Measure; handover is about the owner accepting the controlled process.

distractorExplanations.a: Reporting final results is what lagging indicators do; leading indicators warn before outcomes.
distractorExplanations.b: Leading indicators supplement the primary Y; the project is still judged on the Y itself.
distractorExplanations.d: Spec limits come from customer requirements; leading indicators predict performance early.

options.c: Start a new project charter at once

distractorExplanations.a: Widening control limits hides the signal; limits are recalculated only after a real, intended change.
distractorExplanations.b: Closing the project with fading gains leaves the problem unsolved; controls must be restored first.
distractorExplanations.c: A new charter is premature; first reanalyze why the existing controls failed and restore them.

distractorExplanations.a: Lessons learned are blame-free knowledge capture, not individual performance appraisals.
distractorExplanations.c: Monitoring data belongs to the control plan; lessons learned record what to repeat or avoid.
distractorExplanations.d: Benefit totals are tracked by finance/benefit tracking; lessons learned capture know-how.

distractorExplanations.a: Gage repeatability is an MSA result from Measure, not the business impact benefit tracking checks.
distractorExplanations.b: Training completion is a control activity; benefit tracking validates realized savings and results.
distractorExplanations.d: A significant test result does not confirm realized dollars; benefit tracking measures actual impact.

distractorExplanations.a: Gage changes are technical MSA issues; change management addresses people accepting new ways of working.
distractorExplanations.c: Spec revisions are document/engineering changes, not the people side that change management targets.
distractorExplanations.d: Capital budgets are financial approvals; change management builds stakeholder buy-in and adoption.

distractorExplanations.b: Showing every metric dilutes attention; dashboards should highlight the vital few measures.
distractorExplanations.c: Audit trails come from records and document control, not from cluttered dashboard displays.
distractorExplanations.d: Dashboards never substitute for going to the gemba to see the actual process firsthand.
